title: Mets owner Steve Cohen paid $450 million for Tarik Skubal. His fellow MLB owners want to stop him from doing it again | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

The New York Mets signed starting pitcher Tarik Skubalbecause nothing makes more sense.

Wanting Skubal is simple: He is arguably the best pitcher in the sport right now – a 30-year-old two-time Cy Young Award winner and the most valuable pitcher over the past three seasons, who has allowed one run or fewer in half of his starts during that span.

In a free agent class with very few headliners, Skubal was the most obvious way to make a team markedly better. And no team is more desperate to do so than the Mets.

It has now been 40 years since their last World Series title, a lengthy drought even without grading on the New York-curve of enhanced expectations. When Steve Cohen bought the team ahead of the 2020 season, he said that he would be disappointed to not win a championship in the next three to five seasons. He has since said he regrets that quote, but he almost certainlyisdisappointed – especially after fielding a top-three payroll in the sport the past six seasons. They made the postseason only two of those years, and most recently finished last in their division.

A lot went wrong for the 2026 Mets, perhaps chiefly their plan to forgo a proven ace. And so they signed Skubal because it addresses that need as well as any single move could.

They paid him, reportedly, a record-setting $450 million over nine years – the record is for both the total dollar amount ever awarded to a pitcher and the highest average annual value for a pitcher – because that’s what an already artificially limited market deemed he was worth.

Last year, while still under team control with the Detroit Tigers, Skubal was among the top paid pitchers in the sport after winninga historic arbitration case to earn $32 million. Even without the opportunity to negotiate with anyone other than his current employer, Skubal made record-setting money.

That is to say, yes, baseball players make a lot of money. You could label it obscene, if you were talking about it in the context of the world outside of sports. But within the industry, an independent panel of three experts deemed Skubal worth more than $30 million a year.

Now he’ll make $50 million a year for essentially all of his 30s.

Maybe it’s an “overpay” in that it surpassed projections and expectations, and also it’s just so much damn money. But if you’re determined to get a deal done – as the Mets were, as they should have been given their circumstances – sometimes you simply have to spend more than anyone else is comfortable spending.

That’s also how and why Skubal signed with the Mets: They are owned by the105th richest person on the planet. At least until the Los Angeles Angels’ sale to Stan Kroenke is finalized, Cohen is the richest owner in the sport. Two years before making Skubal the highest paid pitcher, he made Juan Soto the highest paid athlete in America with a 15-year, $765 million contract.

It is a fact that has shaped the narratives around the Mets in recent years at least as much as their underperformance, and especially in conjunction.

Now – with the expiration of the current collective bargaining agreement looming and the league aggressively pushing for a salary cap – that discourse has overtaken the sport.

The Mets have spent the last couple seasons inadvertently proving – with a significant assist from the Milwaukee Brewers – that money does not necessarily buy rings. Now, they’re trying to prove that actually it does, if you just keep spending. Meanwhile, MLB argues that to have such unmitigated effort rewarded would be akin to breaking the sport.

The league would have you believe that Cohen’s Mets signing Skubal is why the Pittsburgh Pirates, for instance, haven’t made the postseason the past 11 seasons. Or why the Tigers traded him last season while just two-and-half games out of a playoff spot.

The owners, a group that includes Cohen, want a salary cap that would prohibit the kind of contracts and the style of team-building that has defined the billionaire’s stewardship of the Mets. Under the current economic structure of the sport, Cohen is not forced to give Skubal $450 million. He did it because he seems to genuinely want to win, and because he can afford to.

The idea that the players should sacrifice earning potential to save billionaires from themselves – helping the billionaires to prioritize their bottom line instead of allowing them to prioritize fielding a competitive team (arguably a different, and more compelling, manifestation of self-interest) – is, understandably, sort of insulting to the MLB Players Association.

Some fans, however, are primarily concerned with whether all 30 ownerscouldhave afforded to sign Skubal.

It’s a reasonable question. Bob Nutting, the Pirates’ owner, for instance does not even crack Bloomberg’s rankings of the wealthiest people in the world. The ownership class across sports has seen a shift from the mega-wealthy to the über-wealthy (assuming that’s bigger?), which has created stratification. Baseball’s payroll disparity is real and undeniable.

But, to continue our juxtaposition, the Pirates don’t have to beat the Mets to make the postseason. They play in different divisions. They do, however, have to at least make a reasonable run at the Brewers, residents of baseball’s smallest market and owners of the best record in baseball the past two years. Neither do the Tigers, who finished fourth in their non-Mets division, behind three teams with smaller payrolls.

A salary cap would change things. This analysis wouldn’t exist. There would be no record-setters in the offseason. No headline-worthy numbers. The economic landscape of the sport would be more homogeneous, which is to say, it would be less interesting.

The Mets would still have sky-high expectations because that’s what four decades of near-misses in the nation’s biggest media market does to a team, but without the added juiciness of a towering payroll standing as a testament to their desperation.

And if, indeed, this pile of money pays off and the Mets win it all – with a roster spanningthree 2026 Rookie of the Yearcandidates to the highest paid position player and pitcher in the sport – it will be hard to believe that wanting it so much and trying so hard was bad for baseball.

At least not as bad as missing games in pursuit of a salary cap would be.
